phonemes.desc: Voiceless velar [k] plus open-mid [e], bearing the acute accent on the first syllable, exactly as LSJ prints it.
Voiced bilabial stop [b] plus short [e]; the middle syllable is light and unaccented.
Alveolar trill [r], short rounded [o], voiceless [s]; the nominative ending of the masculine noun.

pronunciation.approximation: KAIR-beh-ros — the acute falls on the first syllable; sound the final -ros with a light trill.
pronunciation.note: Greek Κέρβερος is proparoxytone — the accent rests on the first syllable, exactly as LSJ prints it. The restoration Kérberos keeps that acute; the ASCII "Cerberus" is the Latinized form that lost it. The etymology is genuinely dark: the old comparison with Sanskrit śárvara ("spotted," one of Yama's two hounds) is famous but unproven, and Beekes (EDG) treats the word as likely Pre-Greek. Tier-2 by rule: the single feature preserved is the accent.

kin.label: Proposed cognate
kin.form: Sanskrit śárvara, "the spotted," a hound of Yama — the comparison is famous, the proof elusive

domains.title: The Hound of Hades
domains.subtitle: The Fifty Heads, the Brazen Voice, and the Gate of No Return
domains.lead: Kérberos is the watch-dog of the dead: Hesiod's brazen-voiced, fifty-headed hound of Hades, who fawns on every soul that enters and devours any that tries to leave — the boundary of the underworld made flesh, fur, and teeth.

cards.name: The Fifty Heads
cards.desc: Hesiod's count in the Theogony; the painters usually settle for three, and the poets keep multiplying.

cards.name: The Brazen Voice
cards.desc: Chalkéophōnos — bronze-throated: the bay of the underworld that the poets heard as metal.

cards.name: The Chain of Heracles
cards.desc: The twelfth labor: dragged to the daylight without weapons, shown to Eurystheus, and taken home again.

cards.name: The Gate
cards.desc: He stands inside the doors of Hades — welcome laid out for the entering, ruin for the leaving.

symbols.name: The many heads
symbols.meaning: Watchfulness that cannot be flanked: every approach covered, every exit denied

symbols.name: The mane of serpents
symbols.meaning: The poets and painters crest him with snakes — the underworld's own fur

symbols.name: The honeyed cake
symbols.meaning: The Sibyl's drugged sop in the Aeneid: the one bribe the gate accepts

symbols.name: The chain of Heracles
symbols.meaning: The only leash ever to hold him — the hero’s bare-handed grip, remembered on vases from the sixth century BCE

mythology.lead: Kérberos' myths are the myths of every threshold that must not be crossed — the one-way gate of Hades, the hero who chains it, and the musicians and magicians who slip past it — and together they are the West's oldest anatomy of a boundary.

myths.title: Born of Typhon and Echidna
myths.text: Hesiod sets him in the monstrous brood of Typhon and Echidna (Theogony 306–312): first Orthrus, the hound of Geryon, then “Cerberus the flesh-eater, the brazen-voiced hound of Hades, fifty-headed, shameless and strong,” and after him the Lernaean Hydra and the Chimaira — with the Nemean lion and the Sphinx of Thebes among the family's cousins. It is the underworld's kennel and armory in a single bloodline: wherever the myths need an impossible guardian, one of Echidna's children is already on duty. Fifty heads is Hesiod's number, and the earliest vase-painters modestly drew two or three; the tradition never settles, because the point is not arithmetic but totality — a watchfulness with no blind side. The genealogy also fixes his allegiance from birth: sired by the storm-giant who once stormed Olympus, he ends up as Hades' doorman, the monster employed by order. His family makes monsters; his job is to keep them in.

myths.title: The Porter of the Dead
myths.text: Later in the same poem (Theogony 767–773) Hesiod gives the hound his job description: Kérberos waits before the dark house of Hades and dread Persephone, and on those who come in he fawns with his tail and both ears — but he lets none go back out; he watches, and devours whomsoever he catches passing the gates. It is the earliest full portrait of the boundary's one-way logic: courtesy inward, annihilation outward. The detail that he fawns — tail wagging, ears flat — is stranger and better than mere ferocity: the gate of death is not cruel, only absolute. Everyone is welcome to enter, and no one is allowed to leave; hospitality and appetite are the same policy seen from different sides. Every later descent-katabasis narrative in Greek, and arguably in the West, inherits this grammar — Charon's fare, the rivers, the judges — but the dog was there first, holding the door in the oldest written map of the Greek underworld.

myths.title: The Twelfth Labor
myths.text: The last and hardest labor set by Eurystheus was to bring the hound up from the dead. Apollodorus (Library 2.5.12) tells it plainly: Heracles descended — through the cave at Tainaron in the southern Peloponnese, Pausanias notes (3.25.5), though Heracleia Pontica claimed the same honor — asked Hades for the dog, and was given leave to take him if he could master him without weapons. Wrapped in the lion's skin, Heracles grappled Kérberos until the hound yielded, led him up into the light, and showed him to Eurystheus, who hid in his bronze storage jar — then dutifully carried him back down again. Homer already knows the tale: the Odyssey (11.623–626) remembers Heracles' fetching “the hound of the loathed king of the underworld,” and the Iliad remembers the wound Hades took at Pylos over the same expedition. The labor completes the hero's curriculum: having visited every extremity of the living world, he is sent for its door itself — and brings it home on a chain, briefly, as proof.

myths.title: Charmed and Drugged
myths.text: Music succeeded where force was not asked to try. In Virgil's Georgics (4.483) Orpheus' song holds Kérberos gaping, his three mouths stilled and his jaws relaxed, as the poet walks the path toward Eurydice. A generation of readers later the Aeneid (6.417–423) gives the Sibyl the practical method: a cake sopped in honey and soporific drugs, tossed into the three ravenous throats, which sink the watchdog into sprawled unconsciousness while Aeneas slips past. Force, song, and pastry: the three keys the tradition cuts for the one lock the dead cannot pick. The Aeneid's detail is the more honest one — the sop is a bribe paid to a functionary, and the Sibyl treats the hound less as a monster than as customs. Both versions agree on the rule that governs every threshold: what cannot be overpowered can sometimes be put to sleep, and what cannot be put to sleep can sometimes be sung through — but the gate itself never opens both ways.

lore.syncretism: Rome naturalized him wholesale — Virgil, Ovid, Horace, and Statius all keep him at his post — and Dante demoted him to overseer of the third circle, the three-throated beast clawing the gluttons in the rain until Virgil clogs his throats with earth. His real cross-cultural argument is etymological: the nineteenth century matched him with Yama's spotted hounds of the Ṛgveda (śárvara), a comparison that would make him the oldest watchdog in the Indo-European family; Beekes and the modern handbooks prefer a Pre-Greek origin and leave the match unproven. Either way, the shape of him — the plural-headed guardian of a gate that opens only inward — recurs wherever the dead need keeping.
lore.culturalLegacy: "Cerberus" is the living language's word for the guardian who cannot be bought: firms, firewalls, and customs houses borrow the name when they want menace with seniority. His labor completed Heracles' curriculum and fixed the katabasis as the hero's final exam, and his three throats gave painters, from black-figure vase-men to modern film, the underworld's most durable mascot. The restoration Kérberos returns the name to its Greek accent — the Latinized Cerberus had been wearing Rome's pronunciation for two thousand years.
lore.extendedMeditation: Kérberos is courteous to everything that accepts the terms and merciless to everything that argues with them. Every threshold worth having — a discipline, a vow, a border of the self — keeps some form of him: the part of the gate that cannot be reasoned with, because reasoning is not its job. The question he asks every visitor is the simplest one: are you here to stay, or are you here to leave — because only one of those is offered.

sources.name: Beekes, R. S. P., Etymological Dictionary of Greek, s.v. Κέρβερος (Brill, 2010).

lore.archaeology: Greek art drew him early and often: black-figure vases of the sixth century BCE show Heracles leading the hound on a chain, usually with two or three heads though Hesiod says fifty, and the type persists through the Caeretan hydriai and Attic red-figure. The Greeks pointed to real descents: the cave at Cape Tainaron in the southern Peloponnese was shown as the mouth by which Heracles dragged him up (Pausanias 3.25), and Heracleia Pontica claimed the same honor on the Black Sea. His lines in the Theogony remain the oldest written portrait of the underworld's watch-dog.
